choices.label: Bring the sudden chest-discomfort concern to the ED senior now and assign owners while the cause is clarified.

choices.label: Complete the diagnostic worklist first, then decide which clinician should receive the concern.
choices.feedback: A fuller record may refine the differential, but it does not supply an owner for the concern in the meantime. Ask the ED senior to accept review while the information develops.

choices.label: Restate the chest-discomfort concern, distinguish reviewed from pending information, and confirm the ED senior responsible for the next review.

choices.label: Let completion of the remaining worklist determine when somebody next reviews the patient.

variants.prompt: The ECG report you reviewed describes a small, nonspecific ST change in aVL. How should that report affect your reassessment message?

choices.label: Use the ST change to hand over a confirmed coronary cause and set aside the aortic question.
choices.feedback: The supplied ECG is nonspecific. Treating it as confirmation would overstate this report and erase a competing concern without addressing its evidence.

choices.label: A routine chest-pain referral queue, without a named receiving clinician.

situation.prompt: Which statement can you support from the opening handoff or a finding you actually reviewed?

choices.label: A 61-year-old arrived with sudden severe chest discomfort; the initial handoff was incomplete.
choices.feedback: These are opening facts. They are enough to communicate a concern without claiming an unreviewed examination or scan.

choices.label: The reviewed history describes pain maximal at onset and radiating to the back.
choices.feedback: This adds only the history you reviewed; it is a concerning pattern, not proof of one cause.

choices.label: The reviewed examination records different pressures in the two arms.
choices.feedback: This examination finding belongs in the handoff once reviewed. Its significance remains part of the clinical assessment.

choices.label: The reviewed CTA report describes an ascending-aortic intimal flap extending into the arch.
choices.feedback: This is a report-specific statement. It is available only after that report has been reviewed.

choices.label: The opening chest discomfort establishes a coronary cause.
choices.feedback: The opening symptom raises concern but does not establish that cause. Keep the observation separate from the working explanation.

uncertainty.prompt: Which qualification keeps the handoff within the evidence you have?

choices.label: Chest discomfort in the opening handoff does not establish a cause; any stronger claim must cite a reviewed finding.

choices.label: The reviewed small, nonspecific ECG change does not settle the cause of the presentation.
choices.feedback: This limits the ECG observation to what the supplied report supports.

choices.label: The reviewed CTA supports the aortic finding in this story; it does not settle every later care decision.

choices.label: The handoff must wait until a single cause has been confirmed.
choices.feedback: Uncertainty is information to communicate. It is not a reason to leave the concern without an identified receiver.

choices.feedback: This assigns a next review and an update route without predicting a change or selecting treatment.

choices.label: Ask the ED senior which specialist receives the reviewed CTA concern and who remains responsible until the transfer is acknowledged.
choices.feedback: The report supports a focused transfer, but responsibility should not disappear between sender and receiver.

choices.label: Assume responsibility has transferred as soon as the diagnostic requests are sent.

choices.label: “Noted in the worklist; someone will pick up the next result.”
choices.feedback: This acknowledges a message without repeating the concern or identifying who accepted the next review. Clarify those points with the receiver.

actions.label: Build the symptom timeline
actions.finding: Authored fictional history: abrupt chest pain was maximal at onset and moved through to the back.
actions.interpretation: The onset and radiation are high-risk features, but they do not identify one diagnosis by themselves.

actions.label: Perform a focused examination
actions.finding: Authored fictional measurement: arm pressures are 178/105 on the right and 142/88 on the left; the difference is reproducible.
actions.interpretation: The fictional inter-arm difference increases concern for an aortic process and keeps premature coronary anchoring unsafe.

actions.label: Review the ECG
actions.finding: Authored fictional tracing: a small, nonspecific ST change is present in aVL without a complete diagnostic pattern.
actions.interpretation: This finding keeps acute coronary syndrome in the differential but is not decisive and cannot erase the aortic warning signs.

actions.label: Review the chest radiograph
actions.finding: Authored fictional radiograph: the mediastinal contour is described as subtly widened, with no single definitive answer.
actions.interpretation: A plain chest radiograph cannot exclude acute aortic syndrome; this fictional image is an ambiguity-preserving clue, not a diagnosis.

actions.label: Obtain CT angiography of the aorta
actions.finding: Authored fictional CTA report: an intimal flap is seen in the ascending aorta and extends into the arch.
actions.interpretation: In this fictional episode, the CTA is the decisive clue favoring acute aortic syndrome over the competing hypotheses.

actions.label: Make a specialist handoff
actions.finding: The fictional handoff carries the symptom report and CTA finding; it does not imply that other observations were performed.
actions.interpretation: A structured handoff preserves uncertainty and the decisive clue for human review; it does not model treatment or outcome.

openingFacts.label: Sudden severe chest discomfort in the opening handoff

uncertaintyOptions.label: The opening symptom does not identify one cause.
The nonspecific ECG finding does not settle the cause.
The CTA supports an aortic finding; it does not settle every aspect of care.

transfer.prompt: A different fictional patient has sudden severe chest pain. The CTA report says motion obscures the ascending aorta and calls that segment nondiagnostic. No definite flap is reported. Which conclusion best respects this evidence?

choices.label: The absence of a reported flap excludes an aortic process.
choices.feedback: A nondiagnostic segment is not a reliable negative finding. The report explicitly limits what can be concluded.

choices.label: The aortic question remains unresolved; the team needs to clarify the inadequate study.
choices.feedback: The limitation matters. Image acquisition and motion affect diagnostic confidence, so an inadequate segment cannot carry an exclusion claim.

choices.label: The symptom pattern alone confirms dissection despite the report.
choices.feedback: The symptoms justify concern, not certainty. The fictional report has not established the diagnosis.

actions.label: Ask what changed at dinner
actions.finding: Fictional witness account: speech was normal a moment earlier. Word-finding difficulty and right-hand weakness began together and persist.
actions.interpretation: Sudden speech and one-sided movement changes call for urgent assessment, not a wait-and-see conclusion.

actions.label: Read the team examination
actions.finding: Fictional examination: the clinician records difficulty naming familiar objects and right-arm drift. The patient remains awake.
actions.interpretation: The observed pattern strengthens concern but does not establish its cause alone.

actions.label: Read the blood glucose result
actions.finding: Fictional measurement during the symptoms: blood glucose is 106 mg/dL (5.9 mmol/L).
actions.interpretation: This result does not support low glucose as the current explanation; it does not itself prove stroke.

actions.label: Read the first scan report
actions.finding: Fictional non-contrast head CT report: no hemorrhage is seen; no definite early infarct is visible.
actions.interpretation: An early CT without a visible infarct does not rule out ischemic stroke.

actions.label: Read the later imaging review
actions.finding: Fictional team review: diffusion MRI shows a small acute left frontal infarct corresponding to the speech and right-arm changes.
actions.interpretation: The matching imaging finding supports ischemic stroke in this authored story; it is not a rule that every suspected stroke needs MRI before action.

actions.label: Pass on the witness account
actions.finding: The fictional handoff preserves the witnessed onset and persisting changes. It makes no claim about examinations or scans you did not read.
actions.interpretation: A useful handoff separates what was witnessed from what remains unknown.

reasoning.limitationLabel: Compare explanations or identify a limit
reasoning.prompt: Explain how a finding you read supports your concern, how the alternatives compare, and what the record still cannot establish.
reasoning.caseLearningText: Weakening one explanation does not prove another. Connect each collected finding to the concern it supports or weakens, and keep a working hypothesis provisional when decisive evidence is absent.
reasoning.insufficientCitationFeedback: Your route includes the matching fictional imaging finding. Cite that finding to support the conclusion rather than an earlier concern or a result that only weakens a rival.

choices.label: Give the receiving ED team the sudden speech and hand-use changes now, including what you do and do not know.

choices.label: Hold back the witness account until the clinical team has a test result explaining the cause.

choices.label: Describe what this CT report says, while retaining its limit: no visible early infarct on this scan does not exclude early ischemia. Keep any later reviewed findings separate.
choices.feedback: This is a limit of the particular CT report, not a claim that all imaging is inconclusive. As a witness, you can check that the team heard the report accurately while clinicians own its interpretation and care decisions.

choices.label: Tell the receiver that the CT has ruled out stroke because it shows neither hemorrhage nor a visible early infarct.
choices.feedback: That conclusion goes beyond the supplied report. An early ischemic change may not be visible on the first CT, so the report must not be relabeled as excluding stroke.

choices.label: The ED nurse or clinician receiving the speech and hand-use concern.
choices.feedback: This places the account with the team handling the current assessment.

choices.label: A routine primary-care message to be read after the emergency visit.
choices.feedback: That may be a later communication channel, but it does not confirm that the current ED receiver heard the witnessed change.

choices.feedback: This reports the wording of a reviewed scan rather than claiming that all causes have been excluded.

choices.label: The later imaging review I read describes a matching acute left frontal infarct.
choices.feedback: This is available only after that supplied review has been read. An early witness handoff does not require it.

choices.label: The fork difficulty was an ordinary hand slip, so the speech change need not be part of the handoff.
choices.feedback: That explains away an observation rather than reporting it. The receiver needs the speech and hand-use changes together.

choices.feedback: This limits the witness claim without suggesting that a later reviewed report must be ignored.

choices.feedback: This distinguishes a result that weakens one explanation from proof of another.

choices.label: No early infarct visible on the reviewed CT does not exclude an early ischemic stroke.
choices.feedback: This preserves a limit of the supplied CT report; it does not ask the witness to determine clinical management.

choices.label: Because help is already on the way, the ED team no longer needs the initial symptom description.
choices.feedback: An emergency response does not replace the witness information. Make sure the receiving team has heard it.

nextOwner.prompt: What should you confirm about the next review and further family concerns?

choices.label: Ask the ED nurse or clinician who owns reassessment and whom the family should tell if speech or hand use changes again.
choices.feedback: The ED team owns clinical reassessment. You can ask for a clear route to report another observation without predicting that one will occur.

choices.label: Leave reassessment to whoever happens to see the next result, without identifying a receiver for family updates.
choices.feedback: An unnamed future reader is not a confirmed contact. Ask the current team who will receive the next concern.

actions.label: Clarify the recent history
actions.finding: Fictional history: thirst and frequent urination started before the vomiting. There is no established diabetes diagnosis in the record.
actions.interpretation: The chronology weakens a stomach-only explanation but cannot settle the metabolic diagnosis.

actions.label: Read the bedside observations

choices.feedback: This is a student synthesis and an ownership check. It does not turn one reviewed result into a complete diagnosis or an independent care decision.

choices.label: Treat the first available result as completion of the assessment and leave further review to the laboratory worklist.
choices.feedback: A result arriving is not the same as clinical reassessment. The supervisor still needs to know the information reviewed and what needs follow-up.

variants.prompt: You reviewed a plasma glucose of 286 mg/dL. What can you carry into the supervised reassessment from this report?

choices.label: Raised glucose is one component. Bring the ketone and acid-base findings into the synthesis separately; this glucose value alone is not the complete ketoacidosis argument.
choices.feedback: Keep the laboratory components distinct and then connect the reports you actually reviewed. This remains true if you have already read the complete pattern: the diagnosis is supported by their combination, not by glucose alone.

choices.label: Report that the glucose value by itself establishes the complete ketoacidosis pattern, so ketone and acid-base information would not change the synthesis.
choices.feedback: The glucose result does not establish the full pattern by itself. Ketone and metabolic-acidosis evidence answer separate questions, even when all reports are already available.

receiver.prompt: Who should accept your synthesis and the next clinical review?

choices.label: The supervising clinician responsible for this assessment.
choices.feedback: This names a receiver with clinical responsibility while preserving the student’s role.

choices.label: The laboratory results inbox, without directly notifying the supervisor.
choices.feedback: A results inbox is not a clinician accepting the concern or responsibility for the next review.

situation.prompt: Which statement uses only opening facts or findings you actually reviewed?

choices.label: A 26-year-old arrived with vomiting, fatigue and abdominal discomfort; the initial stomach-illness account was incomplete.
choices.feedback: This is enough for an early supervisor handoff. It does not claim a laboratory pattern you have not reviewed.

choices.label: The reviewed history places thirst and frequent urination before vomiting, with no established diabetes diagnosis in the record.
choices.feedback: This adds the recorded chronology rather than assuming that the opening complaint settled the cause.

choices.label: The glucose report I reviewed records 286 mg/dL; that number alone is not the entire metabolic pattern.
choices.feedback: This gives a reviewed result and limits the inference from it.

choices.label: I reviewed glucose 286 mg/dL, blood ketones 4.8 mmol/L, and acid-base values of pH 7.22 and bicarbonate 13 mmol/L together.
choices.feedback: This statement becomes available only when all three reports were reviewed. It is not required for an early handoff.

choices.label: The vomiting establishes a stomach illness as the cause of the whole presentation.
choices.feedback: The opening complaint does not establish that explanation. Communicate the symptoms and what is known separately from the working hypothesis.

uncertainty.prompt: Which qualification fits a supervised synthesis without overstating the known evidence?

choices.label: Vomiting and discomfort alone do not confirm a gastrointestinal or metabolic cause; any stronger claim must cite reviewed evidence.
choices.feedback: This remains a true limit of the opening account even after later findings become available.

choices.label: The reviewed glucose value is one component; ketone and acid-base information must be considered separately.
choices.feedback: This does not falsely say that the other reports are still missing if you have also reviewed them.

choices.label: The combined reviewed pattern supports ketoacidosis in this case; its precipitant and care decisions still require the supervisor’s assessment.
choices.feedback: A complete recorded pattern can strengthen the synthesis without transferring independent clinical authority to the student.

choices.label: The initial stomach-illness description is enough to leave competing explanations out of the handoff.
choices.feedback: That would turn the opening suggestion into a confirmed account. The supervisor needs the distinction between symptoms, findings and inference.

nextOwner.prompt: How should follow-up of the concern and later information be assigned?

choices.label: Confirm that the supervising clinician owns reassessment of the presenting concern; bring new reports or symptom changes back through the agreed route.
choices.feedback: The student tracks and communicates information while the supervisor accepts clinical review. A future change is a contingency, not an event the game has simulated.

choices.label: Treat the laboratory worklist as the owner of the next review and wait for every report before updating the supervisor.
choices.feedback: Task completion does not assign clinical responsibility. The supervisor should know what has been reviewed and what still needs attention.

readback.prompt: Which supervisor reply lets you verify the concern and responsibility before ending this handoff?

choices.label: “I heard the vomiting, fatigue and abdominal discomfort concern. I own the next review; distinguish the findings you reviewed from those still pending and bring updates back to me.”
choices.feedback: Verify the repeated concern and next review owner, and correct any mismatch. This confirms communication, not a finalized diagnosis or treatment plan.

choices.label: “The laboratory worklist is visible; whoever sees the final result can complete the assessment.”
choices.feedback: The concern and next clinical owner have not been repeated or accepted. Clarify them with the supervising clinician.

sources.title: WHO Emergency Care Toolkit: Interagency Integrated Triage Tool
sources.scope: Prioritizing clinical concern separately from establishing a diagnosis. These role-specific exercises do not implement or validate a triage scale.

sources.title: NICE CG50: recognising and responding to deterioration
sources.scope: Clinical concern, response ownership and reassessment. No physiological thresholds, observation intervals or treatment instructions are introduced.

sources.title: AHRQ TeamSTEPPS: Handoff
sources.scope: Communicating known information, uncertainty, responsibility and contingencies, with acknowledgment by the receiver. The scripted handoffs are fictional examples.

sources.title: AHRQ TeamSTEPPS: Check-Back (or Repeat-Back)
sources.scope: Receiver repetition followed by sender verification, including family communication. An acknowledgment does not establish a diagnosis or complete pending tasks.

reviewProvenance.text: The owner reports clinician review of earlier Medical Mysteries material. The reviewed scope, artifact and version have not been verified for this addition. These newly authored workflow profiles have not received separate clinician review.

transfer.prompt: A different fictional patient has dehydration, glucose 720 mg/dL, measured total osmolality 334 mOsm/kg, beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.8 mmol/L, venous pH 7.36 and bicarbonate 23 mmol/L. Which explanation fits this laboratory pattern better?

choices.label: Ketoacidosis, because any very high glucose is sufficient.
choices.feedback: High glucose alone does not establish ketoacidosis. The marked ketosis and acidosis from the earlier case are absent here.

choices.label: A hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state rather than the earlier ketoacidotic pattern.
choices.feedback: This authored pattern combines severe hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality without significant ketosis or acidosis. It contrasts with the three-part ketoacidosis pattern.

choices.label: No major metabolic problem, because the pH is not low.
choices.feedback: A near-normal pH does not make severe hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality harmless. The full pattern matters.

source.title: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: 2024 consensus report
